hints: Start by picturing the job - moving a large volume of water upwards through a tall plant, often pulled under great tension. What kind of internal space and wall strength would make that possible?
Think of two linked ideas: what is missing inside the tube to let water flow freely, and what is added to the wall to stop it collapsing or leaking.
walkthrough:
Link Empty Tube to Easy Flow**
Think of xylem as a water pipe. Mature vessel elements are dead with no cytoplasm, no nucleus and no end walls between cells stacked end to end. That leaves a wide, hollow, continuous lumen. With nothing in the way, water can move with very little resistance and in large volume per unit time.

Link Strengthened Wall to Support Under Tension**
Water is pulled up in the transpiration stream, which puts the column under tension that could suck the tube flat. The cellulose wall is thick and impregnated with lignin, often in rings or spirals. Lignin is very strong and waterproof, so it holds the vessel open for support and stops water leaking out sideways. Cellulose also allows adhesion of water to the wall, helping upward movement.

Final answer: 1. Hollow lumen with no cytoplasm and no end walls forming a continuous tube, giving less resistance to / unimpeded flow of water. 2. Walls thickened / impregnated with lignin in rings or spirals, preventing collapse under tension and waterproofing to prevent water loss.

hints: Compare what the tubes are built from - think about living cells with contents versus hollow tubes built from layers of tissues.
Compare special features for control of flow - think about sieve plates and companion cells in plants versus valves and muscle for vasoconstriction in mammals.
walkthrough:
Compare Building Blocks**
Sieve tubes that carry phloem sap are made of living cells placed end to end. They retain cytoplasm and are connected through sieve plates with pores, plus they need companion cells to stay alive and function. Blood vessels in mammals are different - they are hollow structures made from layers of tissues such as endothelium, muscle and elastic tissue, with no cells blocking the lumen.

Compare Flow Control**
Mammals have three types of blood vessels - arteries, veins and capillaries - forming a closed circulation with blood always staying inside vessels and flowing in one direction. Veins have valves to prevent backflow and vessels can vasoconstrict using muscle. Phloem has only one main conducting type, sieve tubes, with no valves and no vasoconstriction, and flow can change direction depending on source to sink.

Final answer: Sieve tubes are composed of living cells with cytoplasm and sieve plates between cells and associated companion cells, whereas blood vessels are hollow tubes composed of tissues with no cytoplasm in the lumen. Blood vessels form a closed system with unidirectional flow and veins have valves, whereas phloem transport is not enclosed in the same way and does not have valves.

hints: Recall what mitochondria do for any cell and think about why an absorbing root hair cell in the soil might have a higher demand for that product than inner root cells.
Think about how water and mineral ions enter differently - one can move down gradients, the other often has to be pumped against its concentration gradient.
Link the extra product from mitochondria to the specific membrane process used for mineral ion uptake in root hairs.
walkthrough:
Remember the Role of Mitochondria**
Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy that is stored as ATP. More mitochondria means a greater rate of ATP synthesis and more energy available for work.

Spot the Energy-Demanding Job**
Root hair cells absorb mineral ions from soil water where ions are often at lower concentration than inside the cell. That means ions must be moved up their concentration gradient by active transport using carrier proteins, which needs ATP.

Put the Causal Chain Together**
Because root hair cells are specialised for active transport of mineral ions, they need large quantities of ATP. Inner root cells shown do less of this active uptake, so root hair cells contain more mitochondria to supply the extra metabolic energy.

Final answer: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration to synthesise ATP. Root hair cells carry out active uptake of mineral ions against a concentration gradient, which requires metabolic energy from ATP, so increased ATP synthesis is needed.
